item.research_question: Why does the CoCrFeMnNi equiatomic high-entropy alloy fail to form stacking fault tetrahedra (SFTs) or vacancy clusters during high-speed plastic deformation and subsequent annealing, despite having a low stacking fault energy similar to metals where SFTs typically form?
item.processing_route: Vacuum induction furnace fabrication; homogenization at 1473 K for 10 h; rolling to ~50 µm; annealing at 1273 K for 1 h in 10⁻⁵ Pa vacuum; high-speed tearing at 1 m/s (strain rate ~10⁶/s); isochronal annealing from room temperature to 873 K in 100 K increments for 10 min.
item.test_conditions: Dark-field weak-beam transmission electron microscopy (TEM) along [011] direction with g = 200; annealing temperatures up to 873 K; high-speed deformation at ~10⁶/s strain rate.
key_findings: No stacking fault tetrahedra (SFTs) were observed in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA after high-speed deformation or after annealing at 873 K.
The average binding energy of di-vacancy clusters was positive (0.25 eV), indicating a tendency to form.
The average binding energy of tri-vacancy clusters was negative (-0.44 eV), ranging between -0.48 and -0.35 eV, indicating instability.
Binding energies for tetra-vacancy clusters were calculated to be positive, suggesting they can be stable.
In contrast, Ni and Cu showed positive binding energies for di-, tri-, and tetra-vacancy clusters that increased with cluster size.
The inability to form tri-vacancy clusters suppresses defect accumulation and promotes interstitial-vacancy recombination.
Under cascade damage (ion/neutron irradiation), tetra-vacancy clusters can form directly, but growth from excess vacancies is suppressed.
item.mechanism: The instability of tri-vacancy clusters (negative binding energy) prevents the formation of larger vacancy clusters (like SFTs) under conditions without cascade damage (e.g., high-speed deformation). This is attributed to lattice distortion caused by the random occupation of lattice sites by atoms of different sizes (Co/Ni undersized, Cr/Fe/Mn oversized). While tri-vacancy clusters are unstable, tetra-vacancy clusters become stable due to the relaxation of this lattice distortion, allowing them to form only under high-energy cascade damage conditions.
item.limitations: The authors state that there are no reliable experimental data to support the calculated migration energy of single vacancies (0.79 ± 0.12 eV). They also note that the surface of the annealed sample was slightly oxidized, making dark-field weak-beam images unclear. Additionally, the study does not fully explain why tetra-vacancy clusters are stable while tri-vacancy clusters are unstable, calling for further detailed analysis.
item.future_work: It is necessary to analyze in detail why the tetra-vacancy cluster is stable while the tri-vacancy cluster is unstable. The authors also state that the same calculations regarding cascade damage are required for the CoCrFeMnNi HEA, as previous simulations were only done for CoCrFeNi HEA.
quotes: The binding energy of the di-vacancy cluster was positive (average of 0.25 eV), while that of the tri-vacancy cluster was negative (average of − 0.44 eV)
The inability to form a cluster containing three vacancies is attributed to the excellent irradiation resistance of the CoCrFeMnNi HEA.
The instability of the tri-vacancy clusters is attributed to this lattice distortion. On the other hand, the tetra-vacancy clusters are stable due to the relaxation of lattice distortion.
